olm8ij-g54852-d1e103.summary: Rubric: Question 3, 'On human acts, moral habits and virtues'.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e114.summary: States the question: whether a moral act, or any of its circumstances, necessarily argues something added that is really distinct from the first nature of the power. Opening argument for no: acts that come before a habit do not argue anything added, and later acts are of the same kind as earlier ones, so later acts do not argue anything added either.
claims: Earlier and later acts of the same kind are of the same ratio.
Acts preceding a habit argue nothing added.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e134.summary: Second argument, a regress. If something is added, from what was it generated? If from acts, one asks whether those acts argue something added. If not, the point is granted. If so, the question repeats to infinity.
claims: Positing an added habit generated by acts leads to an infinite regress.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e147.summary: Argument that a circumstance does not argue something added. It would be either absolute or relative. It is not absolute, since nothing absolute beyond the substance of the act is posited in a natural act, and acts with different circumstances would otherwise differ in kind. It is not a relation, since a relation is neither the principle nor the term of an action. The paragraph ends with a contrary consideration: what is first undetermined and later determined is not without something added.
claims: A circumstance is neither an absolute addition nor a relation.
What passes from undetermined to determined requires something added.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e172.summary: Argument in the opposite direction. Moral goodness is in an act from its circumstance, and this argues something added, or the act would not be morally good.
claims: Moral goodness is in an act through its circumstance.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e188.summary: Methodological remark (textually corrupt). One must first ask whether virtue exists, a question of fact prior to the question of its nature, and this is best settled from the experience of those who have it.
claims: Whether virtue exists is prior to what it is.
The question is best settled from the experience of the habituated.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e199.summary: Plan of the reply in four points: (1) what the habituated person experiences in acting that no one else experiences; (2) whether these experiences show a real addition; (3) the 'quantity' of that reality, whether absolute, relative, or only a mode; (4) its 'quality', that is, its genus and species, inferred from what is experienced.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e223.summary: Table of the four articles: what the habituated person experiences as added in acting; whether it is real; whether it is absolute or relative; what kind of being it is.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e248.summary: Rubric for Article 1: what the habituated person experiences as added in acting.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e255.summary: Plan of Article 1. Aureol starts from what every habituated person experiences. He will first set aside four features that do not mark the virtuous agent, and then give six that do.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e271.summary: Lists, in a garbled text, the four features to be set aside: the substance of the act, its circumstance, a quality belonging to the intellect, and a quality belonging to the affect.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e285.summary: First feature, the substance of the act. Although an act is an accident, it has its own quiddity, and to grasp that quiddity is to grasp its substance. Aristotle refers to this when he says (Ethics II) that habits are generated from acts.
claims: An act, though an accident, has its own quiddity.
Habits are generated from acts (Aristotle).

olm8ij-g54852-d1e301.summary: Adds, from the same place in Ethics II, that earlier and later acts are of the same species.
claims: Acts before and after the habit are of the same species.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e316.summary: Rubric for Article 2: whether the added thing is real. The content that follows first finishes Article 1's list of four features before reaching this question.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e323.summary: Second feature, the circumstance. 'Circumstance' comes from 'standing around'. The term is better than 'accident', because an accident cannot have an accident. It lies adjacent from outside, as when the act is taken with respect to extrinsic factors such as what and when (Ethics VI, ch. 1).
claims: A circumstance is better so named than called an accident, since accidents have no accidents.
A circumstance relates the act to extrinsic conditions.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e345.summary: Third and fourth features: a quality of the intellect and a quality of the affect. Someone acting by chance does not act virtuously, and someone who acts half-heartedly in a sudden situation is not habituated, so a quality in the intellect is required. The agent must also act by choice, which belongs to the affect. The act and its circumstance make an act virtuous. The qualities of intellect and affect make it virtuously elicited. Aristotle (Ethics II, ch. 4) distinguishes doing something virtuous from doing it virtuously, as a child can say something grammatical without speaking grammatically.
claims: Acting by chance is not acting virtuously.
Act and circumstance make an act virtuous; intellectual and affective qualities make it virtuously done.
Doing the virtuous differs from doing virtuously (Aristotle).

olm8ij-g54852-d1e392.summary: Transition: none of these four shows the addition sought, since they are not experienced only by the virtuous. Aureol will prove this.
claims: The four features do not belong only to the virtuous.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e403.summary: Proof using liberality. Giving is the act of liberality, and a non-liberal person can give as the liberal person does, as far as the substance of the act goes. The non-liberal person can also weigh what is given, to whom, when and so on, as the liberal person does.
claims: A non-liberal person can perform the substance of a liberal act.
A non-liberal person can observe the same circumstances.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e419.summary: Continues the proof for the intellectual and affective qualities. A non-liberal person can give knowingly, for example out of shame. The will is so free that anyone can elicit an act of giving knowingly without any habit. So the four features are found in the non-virtuous as well.
claims: Knowing giving is possible without the virtue.
The freedom of the will allows any act to be elicited without a habit.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e439.summary: A doubt: Aristotle says the virtuous person acts by choosing. Aureol grants this of the virtuous as such, but notes that by certain elicited acts one immediately becomes continent rather than virtuous.
claims: The virtuous act by choosing, but choosing alone may yield only continence.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e452.summary: Aureol gives the six features the virtuous person experiences and others do not, gathered from various places in Aristotle: facility, readiness (pronitas), firmness, steadiness (immobilitas), delight, and acting immediately (repente). These are not the substance, circumstance, or intellectual or affective quality of the act, but qualities of the agent. Without them, even with the four, no virtuous habit is shown. With them, the habit is posited.
claims: Six features mark the virtuous agent: facility, readiness, firmness, steadiness, delight and promptness.
These are qualities of the agent, not features of the act.
They are the signs from which a virtuous habit is inferred.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e478.summary: Objections to each of the six, and Aristotelian support for them. Objections: greater difficulty demands greater virtue. The magnanimous person is naturally slow. Facility and readiness seem redundant. For the brave it suffices not to be saddened. If steadiness were required, no one would be virtuous, since no one always acts. Acting suddenly is foolish, since one should deliberate slowly. Reply: Aristotle sets all six as conditions of acting virtuously. Facility: one who acts with difficulty is not virtuous (Ethics III). Readiness: custom is second nature (Ethics VII). Delight: no one is good who does not rejoice in good works, and pleasure is the sign of an acquired habit (Ethics I, II). Steadiness and firmness: Ethics III. Promptness: habit shows most in sudden situations.
claims: One who acts with difficulty is not virtuous.
Custom is a second nature producing readiness.
Delight in acting is the sign of an acquired habit.
Habit appears most clearly in sudden situations.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e570.summary: Distinguishes the six by what each is relative to. Facility concerns obstacles: difficulty when something hinders, ease when nothing does. Readiness concerns an impulse: however easy lifting a straw is, you are not ready unless something drives you. Delight concerns what is loved, as a friend delights in a friend. Steadiness concerns frequency of acts: fasting and then gorging is not temperance. Firmness concerns constancy: half-hearted action, like stammered speech, is no habit. Promptness concerns a settled purpose: the virtuous person, holding the major premise, concludes at once when the matter arises.
claims: Facility is relative to an obstacle; readiness to an impelling force.
Delight is relative to a loved object; steadiness to frequency; firmness to constancy.
Promptness reflects a settled purpose that concludes at once.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e620.summary: Argues that the six are sufficient, by a division of how the agent relates to the act. Relative to the act and its opposite: facility. Relative to many acts: steadiness, acting virtuously whatever the matter. Relative to a single act in its coming-to-be: firmness, a binding of the agent to the act, which is why habits are needed for meritorious acts. Relative to time: deliberation. Otherwise: promptness. These six, not the four features, distinguish the virtuous from the non-virtuous. A non-habituated person can judge to whom, how and when to give, but is not virtuous unless acting easily; acting with difficulty, one is merely tenacious.
claims: The six conditions are exhaustive, by division of the agent's relations to the act.
Firmness binds the agent to the act; hence habits are needed for meritorious acts.
The six, not the four, distinguish the virtuous person.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e690.summary: Short illustrations of the six: someone who does not act readily is not virtuous; someone saddened in giving is like a seller; someone who does not act steadily and firmly is not virtuous; someone who does not choose at once in a sudden case is not properly virtuous.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e708.summary: Replies to the objections against the six conditions. Facility: the argument commits the fallacy of figure of speech by switching 'with difficulty' to an adverb, and the virtuous do not act by straining. Readiness: the magnanimous person is ready for virtuous works and slow only toward everything else; one slow in everything would be proud. Facility and readiness differ, since facility concerns obstacles and readiness concerns impulse. The brave person rejoices even in dying, joy absorbing sensitive sorrow. Steadiness means steadiness suited to humans in this life, as opposed to acting rarely, not absolute permanence.
claims: The virtuous do not act by straining.
Magnanimity is slow toward non-virtuous matters only.
Facility and readiness are distinct.
The brave rejoice in dying, joy absorbing sensitive sorrow.
Steadiness is the steadiness proper to human beings, not absolute permanence.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e776.summary: Reply on firmness and promptness, and the key conclusion that all six point to one real addition. Firmness and steadiness are not the same. On promptness: the virtuous agent acts through a practical syllogism (Ethics VI). Its major, for instance 'it is good to face death to free the city', is already settled. In a sudden case only the minor is deliberated. Aureol concludes that what grounds promptness is the same real addition that grounds facility, readiness and delight. Firmness is the binding of the power to its act, which an inclining weight produces. Promptness, too, comes from that inclining weight, as greater heaviness makes motion quicker. So the six point to one added thing whose first function is to incline the power, and the other conditions follow from this.
claims: The virtuous person acts through a practical syllogism whose major is already settled.
All six conditions argue one real addition in the power.
That addition's first function is to incline the power; the other conditions follow from it.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e854.summary: Two doubts about habit as inclination. First, what is 'inclining'? It is not an act of the will, since it precedes the act, nor an act in the will from the habit, since then an accident would act on its subject. Second, no natural form inclines to more than one thing, but this inclination is to many acts, so it cannot come from a natural habit.
claims: Inclining seems neither an act of will nor an act of the habit on the will.
Natural forms incline only to one thing.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e881.summary: Reply to the first doubt. Inclining is the act of the habit. Virtue is a kind of weight, as lightness is a weight inclining upward. Its 'inclining' is a formal act, not an elicited one, as being hot is having heat. When one feels heaviness, one experiences the first act of the heavy form, felt as resistance to the opposite motion. So one experiences the weight of a habit as resistance to the opposite act or ease toward the act it inclines to. Alternatively, inclining can be an elicited act, as the liberal person wills by inclination yet wills to deliberate first.
claims: Virtue is a weight in the power.
Inclining is the formal first act of a habit, not an elicited act.
The weight of a habit is experienced as resistance to the opposite act and ease toward its own.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e938.summary: Further reply: inclining is not an accident acting on its subject. The whole power, as habituated, elicits the act together with the habit.
claims: The habituated power as a whole elicits the act; the habit does not act on the power.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e954.summary: Reply to the second doubt. A habit inclines materially to many things but formally to one, as heaviness inclines to the centre though many heavy things tend to different centres. Similarly a virtue's mode set by reason is formally one though found in many matters. Any diversity is numerical, through matter, not formal.
claims: A habit inclines formally to one thing and materially to many.
The rational mode of a virtue is formally one across many matters.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e980.summary: Objection: then matter enters the formal notion of virtue, or else all virtues would be the same, since the mean of reason is the same in all. Reply: different matters diversify the modes of reason, because the acts of agents are in a rightly disposed patient, so the mean differs by matter. Alternatively, a natural form inclines to many things numerically while moving to one at a time.
claims: Different matters diversify the mean of reason and so the virtues.
A natural form can incline to many numerically while moving to one at a time.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1019.summary: How a habit can incline to a universal: it inclines not to the universal but to an undetermined singular, a particular mode of reason. So sight inclines not to universal whiteness, nor to this whiteness, but to whiteness indefinitely.
claims: A habit inclines to an undetermined singular, not to a universal.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1048.summary: Rubric for Article 3: the 'quantity' of the added reality, whether absolute or relative.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1057.summary: Introduces Article 3. The 'quantity' of a reality means whether it is absolute or relative, and its 'quality' means its category. First opinion: habits are only relations, and virtue is formally a relation. Its argument: an effect cannot have more entity than its cause, and the reality of these (the six conditions) is relative, not absolute. Authorities and arguments are offered.
claims: On the first opinion, virtue is formally a relation.
An effect cannot have more entity than its cause.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1092.summary: First argument for the relational view. Bodily virtues are relations, so virtues of the soul are too. Health and beauty are bodily virtues, and Aristotle (Physics VII) says they are relational. Health is formally just a balance of humours, and balance is a relation.
claims: Health is formally a balance of humours.
Bodily virtues are relational (Physics VII).

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1111.summary: More arguments for the relational view. Beauty is the proper arrangement of limbs and colour, which are relations, and the soul needs no more entity for its perfection than the body. Knowledge is a relation, and virtue is to appetite as knowledge is to intellect. What is corrupted with no change in anything absolute is relative, and virtue is corrupted merely by ceasing to act. There is no motion toward virtues, and no motion in relation (Physics VII). If virtues were absolute, Aristotle's argument would prove nothing.
claims: Beauty is a due arrangement of members.
Knowledge is a relation, and virtue is to appetite as knowledge is to intellect.
Virtue is corrupted by cessation of acts without absolute change.
There is no motion toward virtues, as there is none in the category of relation.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1157.summary: A common argument against the relational view: what really inclines something is not a mere relation, and virtue inclines the power. The relationalists reply that inclining can be efficient, which a relation cannot do, or formal, which it can, since inclination is an order to something and so a relation.
claims: A mere relation cannot efficiently incline.
Relationalists hold that relation can incline formally.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1188.summary: Second common argument: what is acquired through acts and through grace is absolute, and virtues are acquired so.
claims: What is acquired by acts and grace is absolute.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1197.summary: The relationalists' reply: a relation cannot be acquired immediately as the term of generation, but it can be acquired as a consequence. A power is first generated, and inclination follows as a consequence.
claims: A relation can be acquired as a consequence of generation, not as its term.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1210.summary: Third common argument: nothing becomes able to act from being unable except by something acting on it. Reply: fire becomes able to act through application, which is a relation, so the same may hold here.
claims: Fire becomes able to act through application, which is a relation.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1226.summary: Aureol's own argument that virtue is something absolute, not a mere relation. The added thing must have as much reality as the six conditions require, and they require something absolute in the power. Readiness requires something absolute by which one goes from not ready to ready. It is not formally inclination. It is a way of standing toward the act and qualifies the act, and a relation does not qualify. Likewise newly arising delight requires a newly arising foundation in the power.
claims: The added thing has as much reality as the six conditions require.
Readiness qualifies the act, and a relation does not qualify.
Newly arising delight requires a new foundation in the power.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1277.summary: Develops the delight argument. On what is the new delight founded? Not on the power and act alone, since both existed before without delight. Not on the act alone, since it passes away. So on something else in the power. If that is absolute, the point is made. If relative, one asks about its foundation, and either regresses to infinity or reaches an absolute foundation.
claims: The foundation of habitual delight is neither the power and act nor the transient act.
A regress of relations must end in an absolute foundation.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1310.summary: Restates the first argument. No one experiences a pure relation such as paternity, though one experiences the generative power. Everyone experiences inclination. So inclination is not a mere relation.
claims: Pure relations are not experienced.
Inclination is experienced, so it is not a pure relation.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1330.summary: Second argument against the relational account. A relation is newly acquired only through a change in its term or foundation. Habitual inclination is acquired with no change in the term, the future act, which does not yet exist. So the change is in the foundation in the power, and this foundation cannot itself be a relation without the same question recurring.
claims: A new relation requires a change in its term or foundation.
Habitual inclination is acquired without change in its term.
Therefore something non-relational in the power changes.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1363.summary: Third argument, against the fire example. A relation of the second or third mode does not make something able to act, though one of the first mode might. The order to the act is of the second or third mode. The approximation of fire is of the first mode, founded on unity of place, and so can contribute causally.
claims: Relations of the first mode can contribute causally; those of the second and third cannot.
Fire's approximation is a first-mode relation.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1381.summary: Replies to the first opinion's arguments. Against the major, Aureol denies that the six modes are relations. On bodily virtues, he reports a reply: they are not relations but presuppose something absolute that follows from relations such as commensuration of limbs, and health follows upon a balance of humours. He rejects this reply too: if bodily virtues were real absolutes, Aristotle's argument that there is no motion to them would fail.
claims: The six conditions are not relations.
The reply that bodily virtues are absolutes following relations undermines Aristotle's argument.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1410.summary: Adds that on the opponents' own view beauty is defined abstractly as the due disposition of limbs (Politics III).

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1418.summary: Aureol's own reply: Aristotle uses 'relative' (ad aliquid) equivocally. Sometimes it means the category of relation, and in that sense health is not relative but absolute. Sometimes it means an absolute disposition of many things rather than of one, in which each part is not said relative to another. A circle is absolute, yet is called relative because it includes many parts. Likewise a house. Order does imply relation, but a circle does not.
claims: 'Ad aliquid' is used equivocally by Aristotle.
Health is not a relation in the categorial sense.
An absolute disposition of many parts, like a circle, may be called relative.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1462.summary: Applies the point to Physics VII. Aristotle means that a bodily virtue is not acquired by motion toward the whole, since a disposition of many parts arises only through change in those parts, as a house's form arises through its parts. So it is with beauty and health, which arise as humours are intensified or remitted. Because such dispositions arrange many parts, they seem relational. On knowledge, it is not merely relation. Aureol rejects the reading that knowledge is a relation identical with its foundation, since a creature's relation to God is part of its essence and the creature is still acquired.
claims: Bodily virtues are acquired by changes in their parts, not by motion to the whole.
Knowledge is not merely a relation.
The creature's relation to God is in its essence, yet the creature is acquired.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1525.summary: Further replies on Aristotle's intention. If knowledge has something real that can end a motion, it does so regardless of its relational content. Aristotle cannot mean there is no real acquisition of bodily and intellectual virtues, since he says virtues come from acts and (De anima II) that habit puts one in active potency to consider. Aureol's interpretation: when Aristotle denies alteration in such cases, he means alteration that destroys, not alteration that perfects. One who becomes knowing is not commonly said to be altered, yet knowledge is acquired.
claims: Aristotle holds virtues and knowledge are truly acquired.
There are two kinds of alteration: destructive and perfective.
Aristotle denies only destructive alteration in the acquisition of virtue and knowledge.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1593.summary: Another solution of Aristotle's argument. Every altering thing touches, and the soul does not touch, so there is no motion in it directly. Virtue is called relative because it includes many things, and one does not first move toward the whole. Moral virtue is acquired through alteration concerning pleasure and sorrow in the sensitive part, but the alteration is not directly toward the virtue. Knowledge likewise is acquired after alteration in memory and the sensitive part, not first in itself.
claims: Moral virtue is acquired through alteration of the sensitive part regarding pleasure and pain, not directly.
Knowledge is acquired after alteration in memory and the sensitive part.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1665.summary: Second opinion: the six conditions argue a true absolute thing added to the natural power. Quantity is a true absolute thing though it bears on measure, so the added quality is a true absolute thing. Just as heaviness is something added on which a relation to object and act is founded, differing formally but not really, so with virtue.
claims: On the second opinion, virtue is a true absolute thing added to the power.
Its relation to act differs from it only formally.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1698.summary: Transition: Aureol will resolve the preceding positions in setting out his own.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1706.summary: Aureol's distinction. 'Absolute' can mean absolute from a term, as opposed to relative, or absolute from a subject, that is, a thing separable in thought from its subject, unlike straightness in a line. Virtue is not something separable from its subject. It is a mode of the subject, like straightness of a line or figure of quantity, not a relation and not something like the 'when' and 'where' categories. Against the objection that straightness is not a quality while virtue is: straightness is in the fourth species of quality.
claims: 'Absolute' means either absolute from a term or absolute from a subject.
Virtue is a mode of the power, not a thing separable from it.
Straightness is in the fourth species of quality.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1758.summary: Develops the analogy with straightness. Straightness is a quality in the line, since it answers 'what kind?', and it makes a composite with the line, as figure does with quantity (Metaphysics VII). An objection holds that the argument fails because one quality being a pure mode does not mean another is.
claims: Straightness answers the question 'what kind?' and so is a quality.
A mode composes with its subject.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1784.summary: Long reply that virtue, like all quality, is a mode. Relative and absolute cannot fall in one genus, and neither can a mode and a thing separable from its subject, so species of one category cannot divide that way. Divine power can separate more than our intuition, but our intellect cannot define straightness without a line or figure without quantity, so these are not separable things. A mode can be a principle 'by which', as the sharpness of a knife modifies it as virtue modifies the act. Every quality is a mode: whiteness whitens formally, neither as a thing plus subject nor as a relation. The six conditions require only that the power be modified, as a polished blade cuts more easily.
claims: A mode and a separable thing cannot be species of one category.
Our intellect cannot define straightness without a line or figure without quantity.
Every quality is a mode of its subject.
A mode can be a principle by which a subject acts.
The six conditions require only that the power be modified.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1884.summary: Reply to the second opinion's first reason: facility needs only a modification. Quantity is nothing but divisibility into parts, so greater divisibility means greater quantity.
claims: Facility requires only a modification of the power.
Quantity is just divisibility into parts.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1895.summary: Further reply: the category of quality is real, not as a thing simply but as a thing that is a mode.
claims: Quality is real as a mode, not as a separable thing.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1904.summary: Raises the remaining difficulty: is the habit absolute from its term? Arguments on both sides. First, for not separable from the term: a thing is placed in its genus by the same thing that distinguishes it from other species, and a habit cannot be understood without its term.
claims: A habit cannot be understood without its term.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1921.summary: Further arguments for the relational element. If a habit included something absolute and something relative, it would not be one, yet a habit is one quality. What varies the species of quality belongs to quality, and the order to a term varies the habit's species, as health and sickness differ by order of humours. Taciturnity is a virtue in a woman and a vice in a prudent man, differing only by fit to the person. Virtue can arise when reason supervenes without any change in the inclination.
claims: Order to a term varies the species of quality.
The same disposition can be virtue or vice depending on fit (taciturnity).
A habit is a single quality.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e1963.summary: More arguments. What distinguishes the four species of quality belongs to the genus, and they are distinguished by order, as softness. On the other side, a habit does not formally include a relation, because the notions of the categories are unmixed. If knowledge formally included a relation, so would grammar, which contradicts Aristotle's Categories. And knowledge would be one per accidens.
claims: The species of quality are distinguished by order.
The notions of the categories are unmixed.
If knowledge included a relation formally, grammar would too, against Aristotle.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2020.summary: Aureol's resolution, first part. A quality not absolute from its term could mean either a composite of an absolute mode plus a relation founded on it, or a single simple mode with its own 'ofness toward this'. The first does not belong to the category of quality, since a species is one simple concept and cannot combine absolute and relative. A merely formal or conceptual distinction would not help, since a relation is really toward another. On that view there would be two genera and two realities.
claims: A quality cannot be a composite of an absolute mode and a relation.
A species is a single simple concept.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2062.summary: Resolution, second part. Some qualities are dispositions 'of this toward that' (such as knowledge), others only 'of this'. Being 'of this toward that' does not include a relation formally, because disposition differs from relation: being 'of this toward that' is not simply being 'toward that'. Readiness is such a disposition toward the act. So virtue is not absolute from its term, yet is a quality, not a relation. To understand straightness one need only understand 'of this'. To understand knowledge or virtue one must understand 'of this toward that'. Hence Aristotle (Physics VII) says virtue is the disposition of the perfect toward the best.
claims: Some qualities are dispositions of something toward something.
Disposition toward something is not a relation.
Virtue is a disposition of the power toward its act, a quality not absolute from its term.
Virtue is the disposition of the perfect toward the best (Aristotle).

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2117.summary: Reply to the argument that whatever belongs to a habit belongs to quality. Granted, and it is 'of this toward that'. It does not follow that it is a relation, because a relation is not a disposition.
claims: A disposition 'of this toward that' is not thereby a relation.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2135.summary: Reply on health. The proportion of qualities is not itself the quality. The mode arising from the humours is health. Different dispositions 'of this toward that' make different virtues.
claims: Health is the mode arising from the humours, not their proportion.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2149.summary: Reply to the next arguments: the habit is not a relation, since it is not a relation of bearing but a disposition with a twofold lack of separability (from subject and from term).
claims: Habit is a disposition inseparable from both subject and term.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2158.summary: Reply about grammar. Grammar includes in its concept a disposition 'of this toward that', namely toward letters. By the force of the word it does not include a relation, which is Aristotle's meaning, as with knowledge.
claims: Grammar includes a disposition toward letters but not a relation.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2171.summary: Final reply: disposition within the genus of quality belongs to the notion of quality, though differently in different dispositions. Virtue is a disposition of this toward that.
claims: Virtue is a disposition of this toward that within the genus of quality.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2199.summary: Rubric for Article 4: what kind of being the added thing experienced by the habituated person is.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2208.summary: Opens Article 4. The added thing is in the genus of quality, in the first species. Aureol first raises a doubt about the genus: Augustine (De moribus Ecclesiae I, 25) seems to say virtues are loves, so a virtue would be a weakened love and knowledge a weakened understanding.
claims: The added thing is in the genus of quality, first species.
Augustine seems to identify virtues with loves.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2230.summary: Further doubt: by experience habits are called affections, and love is in the genus of action. Reply: habits are in the genus of quality. A form is inferred from its formal effect, as heat from heating. The six conditions argue a formal effect in the agent, acting readily, and so a power disposed and inclined. What they include is a disposition and quality.
claims: Habits are in the genus of quality.
A form is inferred from its formal effect.
The six conditions show a disposed and inclined power, hence a quality.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2257.summary: Reply to the Augustinian doubt. Even if virtues were loves, the conclusion would hold, since love signifies a resting form or mode relative to an object. But virtues are not dormant affections. Saying otherwise contradicts experience, which differs for habits and acts. Also, one habit would be destroyed by another's act, as one intense thought drives out another, which does not happen. So habits are modes of the power, expressed by readiness, and qualities. They are called affections because they are inclinations to acts.
claims: Virtues are not dormant acts of love or understanding.
If habits were acts, one would be destroyed by the act of another.
Habits are modes of the power, called affections because they incline to acts.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2299.summary: Turns to the species. Objection: mean and extremes are in the same proximate genus, and virtue is a mean between passions, which are in the third species of quality, so virtue is too. Aureol holds it is in the first species. He reports Simplicius' division of the species of quality: adventitious vs natural; perfecting substance in potency (second species), in act in depth (third), or on the surface (fourth).
claims: Virtue is in the first species of quality.
Simplicius divides the species by origin and by how they perfect substance.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2330.summary: Criticism of Simplicius' division. A respondent answers an objection about order by saying Aristotle did not care about order. Aureol's arguments: the differences dividing a genus must not cross species, yet adventitious figures and virtues cross them. A proper division of forms should not be taken from origin, such as creation versus generation.
claims: Dividing differences must not be found across species.
A division of forms should not rest on their mode of origin.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2365.summary: More against Simplicius. Dividing differences must constitute species through what belongs to the genus, and adventitious and natural do not belong per se to disposition. The same division would apply to relation, making it accidental. Colour is not in depth.
claims: Adventitious and natural do not belong per se to the notion of disposition.
Colour is not in depth.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2387.summary: A second division, from 'another doctor in a Summa': accidents are distinguished by formal notions, and quality's formal notion is termination or mode. The mode can relate to the subject in three ways: by quantity, by the qualitative principles of nature (matter and form), or by nature.
claims: On this view the formal notion of quality is termination or mode.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2409.summary: Continues this division. Quantity is neither good nor bad, neither easily nor hardly movable (fourth species). By principles of nature, through action and passion, the second species. By relation to nature, the first species, which, lacking the notion of end, is divided by good and bad, slow and swift, because motion is nature. So: first by nature, second by action, third by passion, fourth by the subject's quantity.
claims: On this view the four species are ordered by nature, action, passion and quantity.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2441.summary: Further on the first species and criticism. In nature there is motion with speed and slowness, hence easily and hardly movable modes. Criticism: one quality cannot be in both the first and second species, yet human virtues dispose to both nature and operation.
claims: One quality cannot belong to two species.
Human virtues dispose to operation as well as nature.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2470.summary: More criticism. Whiteness taken absolutely is a quality, but in which species? It fits none on this account, since it has no per se order to operation; its order to sense is incidental. And a virtue like taciturnity would be in the first species when it suits a nature and in another when it does not.
claims: Whiteness absolutely taken fits no species on the criticized account.
The same virtue would fall in different species by fit.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2507.summary: Third division, by subjects: dispositions of quantity (fourth species), of body alone (third), of soul (first), or of both together (second). Rejected: beauty, a bodily virtue, is in the first species, against this view. Soft and hard are in the second species yet are not of the composite.
claims: Dividing species of quality by subject fails.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2536.summary: Aureol's own division. Differences must follow formal notions, and the notion of quality is a modifying disposition. Either a disposition 'of this' only (third and fourth species) or 'of this toward that' (first and second). Dispositions 'of this' are divided by what they dispose: substance (second species) and quantity (fourth). Dispositions 'of this toward that' relate a thing to what is or is not its perfection. As perfection, they perfect either inherently (health, beauty) or by inclination through act (virtue, habit). Being good or bad, both are in the first species. So all bodily and vital virtues are in the first species, since virtue is the disposition of the perfect toward the best, its end, which may be operation, as running well belongs to a horse. Taken not as perfection, they concern actions and passions and fall in the third species, as health and sickness as passions, passibility and valetudo.
claims: Quality is a modifying disposition.
Species divide into dispositions 'of this' and 'of this toward that'.
Dispositions toward perfection, inherent or by inclination, fall in the first species.
All bodily and vital virtues are in the first species of quality.
Virtue is the disposition of the perfect toward the best, its end.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2649.summary: Applies the division: what the six conditions argue is in the first species of quality, since it is 'of this toward that' as perfecting, naturally apt to perfect through act and not by inhering.
claims: The habit shown by the six conditions is in the first species of quality.
It perfects through act, not by inherence.

olm8ij-g54852-d1e2660.summary: Reply to the opening argument: circumstances make an act virtuous but not virtuously done, and so likewise with the moral act. The added habit is required for the latter.
claims: Circumstances make an act virtuous but not virtuously performed.

olm8ij-g54852-Dd1e241.summary: Article 1 begins the inquiry into what the habituated person experiences when acting. Aureol plans to set aside four features that do not mark the virtuous agent (the substance of the act, its circumstance, and qualities of intellect and affect) and then give six that do. In the edition's article division, this article contains only the plan, the list of the four, and the first of them: the substance of the act has its own quiddity, habits come from acts, and earlier and later acts share a species (Ethics II). The rest of the discussion runs on under Article 2.
claims: An act, though an accident, has its own quiddity.
Habits are generated from acts of the same species as those that follow.

olm8ij-g54852-Dd1e309.summary: Article 2 is headed 'whether the added thing is real'. It first finishes Article 1's analysis. The circumstance relates the act to extrinsic conditions. Intellectual and affective qualities make the act virtuously done rather than merely virtuous (Aristotle's contrast of grammatical and grammatically). None of the four belongs only to the virtuous, since a non-liberal person can give knowingly and with all the circumstances. Aureol then gives six marks experienced only by the virtuous: facility, readiness, firmness, steadiness, delight and promptness. He grounds them in Aristotle, distinguishes them by their reference points, argues they are exhaustive, and answers objections (the slow magnanimous person, the brave person's sorrow, the virtue of deliberation). The practical syllogism with a settled major explains promptness. All six point to one real addition whose first function is to incline the power like a weight. Inclining is the habit's formal first act, experienced as ease toward the act and resistance to its opposite. It is not an accident acting on its subject, since the habituated power as a whole elicits the act. A habit inclines formally to one rational mode and materially to many matters, and to an undetermined singular rather than a universal.
claims: The substance, circumstance and cognitive and affective qualities of an act are found in the non-virtuous too.
Six conditions mark the virtuous: facility, readiness, firmness, steadiness, delight and promptness.
The six conditions argue one real addition in the power, which inclines it like a weight.
Inclining is the formal first act of a habit, not an elicited act.
A habit inclines formally to one mode of reason and materially to many.

olm8ij-g54852-Dd1e1041.summary: Article 3 asks whether the added habit is absolute or relative. A first opinion holds virtue to be a mere relation. It argues from bodily virtues (health as balance of humours, beauty as proportion), from knowledge, from corruption by mere cessation of acts, and from Aristotle's denial of motion to virtues (Physics VII). Aureol finds the common rebuttals weak but argues that the six conditions require something non-relational. Readiness qualifies the act, which no relation does. New delight needs a new foundation in the power. Inclination is experienced, as pure relations are not. A new relation requires a change in its foundation. He explains Aristotle's 'ad aliquid' as equivocal: health and beauty are absolute dispositions of many parts, like a circle, acquired through changes in their parts. Aristotle denies only destructive alteration in acquiring virtue and knowledge, not perfective alteration. Against a second opinion that virtue is a separable absolute thing, Aristotle's key distinction is between 'absolute from a term' and 'absolute from a subject'. Virtue, like every quality, is a mode of its subject, as straightness of a line or sharpness of a knife, not a separable thing. On the remaining difficulty, virtue is not absolute from its term. It is a single simple disposition 'of this toward that'. That is not a relation, since disposition and relation differ. Hence Aristotle calls virtue the disposition of the perfect toward the best.
claims: Virtue is not a mere relation.
Aristotle uses 'ad aliquid' equivocally; health and beauty are absolute dispositions of many parts.
Aristotle denies only destructive, not perfective, alteration in acquiring virtue.
Every quality, including virtue, is a mode of its subject, not a separable thing.
Virtue is a single disposition 'of this toward that', which is not a relation.

olm8ij-g54852-Dd1e2192.summary: Article 4 asks what kind of being the habit is. It belongs to the genus of quality, in the first species. Against Augustine's apparent identification of virtues with loves, Aureol argues from formal effect: the six conditions show a power disposed and inclined, hence a quality. Virtues are not dormant acts, which experience refutes, and if they were, one habit would be destroyed by another's act. They are modes of the power, called affections because they incline. On the species, he rejects three divisions of the four species of quality: Simplicius' by origin and depth, a 'Summa' division by relation to nature, action, passion and quantity, and a division by subjects. Each fails because its differences cross species or are not per se. His own division: quality is a modifying disposition, either 'of this' (third and fourth species) or 'of this toward that' (first and second). Dispositions toward a thing as its perfection, inherent like health or by inclination through act like virtue, fall in the first species. Taken as actions and passions, they fall in the third. So the habit shown by the six conditions is in the first species. Answering the opening argument, circumstances make an act virtuous but not virtuously done.
claims: The habit is in the genus of quality.
Virtues are not dormant acts but modes of the power.
Quality is a modifying disposition, divided into dispositions 'of this' and 'of this toward that'.
The habit is in the first species of quality, as a disposition perfecting through act.
Circumstances make an act virtuous but not virtuously performed.

olm8ij-g54852.summary: Question 3 of Aureol's commentary on Book III, Distinction 23 (on human acts, moral habits and virtues) asks whether a moral act or its circumstances necessarily argue something really added to the first nature of the power. Aureol proceeds from experience. The substance, circumstances and cognitive and affective qualities of an act can be found in the non-virtuous. Only the virtuous experience six marks: facility, readiness, firmness, steadiness, delight and promptness. These argue one real addition that inclines the power like a weight, experienced as ease and resistance. Against those who reduce virtue to a relation, he argues that readiness qualifies the act, new delight needs a new foundation, and relations are not experienced. He reads Aristotle's 'ad aliquid' in Physics VII as equivocal. Against those who make it a separable absolute thing, he holds that virtue, like all quality, is a mode of its subject: a simple disposition 'of this toward that', which is neither absolute from its term nor a relation. Finally, he places virtue in the first species of quality, a disposition that perfects through act, by his own division of the four species. The article divisions in the printed text do not quite follow the content: Article 2 opens by finishing Article 1's account.
claims: A virtuous habit is shown by six experienced conditions.
These conditions argue a real addition that inclines the power.
Virtue is not a relation but a mode of the power, a disposition 'of this toward that'.
Virtue is in the first species of quality.
